title: LIBRARY TRANSFORMATION IN MALAYSIA From Academic Library to Innovation Ecosystem: PTTA’s Transformation at UTHM
raw_text: A library does not become an innovation hub simply by installing technology or adding new programs. The deeper change happens when it connects people, shares resources, and creates a lasting role across the university. Student Mobility Program Universitas Negeri Jakarta @ Drone Showcase Beyond books and buildings Perpustakaan Tunku Tun Aminah (PTTA), the academic library of Universiti Tun Hussein Onn Malaysia (UTHM), has been widening its role since 2020. Alongside its established responsibilities for collections, information access, study, and research support, the library now brings together technology showcases, cultural heritage, digital systems, student learning, and community engagement. This development reflects a broader change taking place in academic libraries. Users still need reliable access to information, but they also need places to collaborate, experiment, present ideas, preserve shared memory, and connect with expertise across the institution. For PTTA, the challenge has been to support these activities in a technical university where specialist knowledge, equipment, funding, and authority are distributed among many units. Its response has been practical: the library contributes what it already does well, including space, curation, information organisation, visibility, and trusted relationships. title: “Measurement, Evaluation, and Demonstrating Impact of Library Services” A Three-Day IFLA Impact Training Workshop at the University of Lahore
raw_text: The IFLA Impact Training Workshop at the University of Lahore The Learning Resource Center (LRC) and the Department of Information Management at the University of Lahore, Pakistan, organised a comprehensive three-day workshop in collaboration with the International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions (IFLA). Titled “Measurement, Evaluation, and Demonstrating Impact of Library Services,” the workshop was held from 22–24 August 2026 and brought together library and information professionals to develop a deeper understanding of how library services can be evaluated, measured, and communicated through evidence of their impact. A total of 27 participants attended the workshop. The participants included library staff from the Learning Resource Center at the University of Lahore’s main campus and sub-campuses, information professionals from the Department of Information Management, and invited librarians and professionals from other public and private institutions in Pakistan. The participants were selected based on their professional roles, their engagement with library services, and their interest in improving the resources, programmes, and services offered to their communities. The workshop was made possible through the support of the University of Lahore (Pakistan) and IFLA. title: IFLA President and Secretary General visited China

Leslie delivered an opening address at the conference, highlighting that libraries in China are well known at IFLA for their commitment to reading promotion and their creative programmes and marketing campaigns that reinforce the importance of reading. title: Innovating Access: How the University of San Agustin’s Learning Resource Center is Redefining the Student Experience
raw_text: At the University of San Agustin’s Learning Resource Center (USA-LRC) in Iloilo City, Philippines, innovation is treated not as a passing trend but as a deliberate strategy for expanding access, strengthening engagement, and preparing Augustinian students for a digitally driven world. Moving beyond the traditional academic library model, the LRC has introduced three initiatives: Expanded Computer Facilities, the Tablet Loan Service, and the arrival of Monica, the library’s first service robot . Together, these innovations are reshaping how Augustinian students, faculty, researchers, and alumni experience the library. Computer Facilities in the Learning Commons The Learning Commons now houses dedicated computer workstations that support the full range of academic tasks, from research and assignments to online examinations. Each workstation provides direct access to the library’s subscribed databases, letting users move seamlessly from searching scholarly literature to completing their work without leaving their seats. The facility responds to a simple but persistent reality: not every Augustinian student has reliable access to a personal computer. By placing these workstations within the Learning Commons rather than a separate laboratory, the LRC keeps technology access alongside librarians, print collections, and study space, reinforcing that digital and physical resources form one learning environment. title: Myanmar Library Association Successfully Conducts Training to Strengthen Organisational Records and Information Management (RIM) Skills
raw_text: Modernizing the Workplace through RIM Expertise In the modern era, the ability to manage information effectively has become a critical foundation for organisational success. Records serve as an organisation’s institutional memory, evidence of its operations, and a valuable resource for accountability, compliance, and future decision-making. Recognizing these growing needs, the Myanmar Library Association (MLA) successfully conducted a RIM sTraining Programme on May 30, 2026, bringing professional library and information management expertise to the business sector. A Tailored Programme for Business Professionals The training was organised under the leadership of MLA Patron Daw Khin Khin Htun , in collaboration with U Tin Myint, Director of Asia General Holding Co., Ltd. The programme was specifically designed for employees working across different business sectors. Thirty participants representing eight companies attended the training and gained both fundamental and practical knowledge for systematically managing physical and digital records generated in their daily work. title: Championing Inclusivity: Empowering Voices, Elevating Talents
raw_text: In line with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDG), particularly SDG 10 on Reduced Inequalities and SDG 4 on Quality Education, the National Library of Malaysia (NLM) remains deeply committed to transforming modern libraries into barrier-free spaces where every individual, regardless of ability, enjoys equal access to knowledge and community life. As disability rights advocate Judith Heumann once profoundly stated, “Inclusion is not a strategy to help people fit into the system and structure which exists in our societies; it’s about transforming those systems and structures to make it better for everyone.” Grounded in this belief, the library has spent the past year championing social inclusion by fostering talent development among Persons with Disabilities (PWD), nurturing local literary appreciation and upgrading accessibility infrastructure to ensure no reader is left behind. A major milestone in this mission was the Open Day with PWD program, an initiative specially curated to celebrate talents within the PWD community through reading literacy and Malay literature enrichment. The event provided a dynamic platform for PWD participants to showcase their creative abilities through a Malay folklore storytelling competition, poetry recitations centered on unity and nationhood, and Braille reading performances. A 1,000-mile cloud on Mars may reveal physics never seen in nature
raw_text: Every morning during the Martian spring and summer, a thin and extremely long cloud emerges, only to disappear again. The wispy formation appears near the volcano Arsia Mons and gradually elongates until it reaches over 1,000 miles—about the distance from New York to Kansas City as the crow flies—before dissipating. This cycle then repeats for several months. Since it was first recorded by a probe in 2018, scientists have been unable to find a plausible explanation for the existence of this cloud, often referred to as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC). Until now. Recently, researchers successfully modeled the cloud’s formation for the first time, their results suggesting that it may be driven by a physical process that has never been directly observed in any planet's atmosphere. "We found that we needed to include some exotic physics… physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature. It certainly hasn’t been seen in action before," Jorge Hernández-Bernal, a planetary scientist at Paris’ Sorbonne Université and lead author of the study, said in a press release . "Once we included this physics in our simulations, the AMEC emerged just as we hoped.” Read full article Comments

Ice sheet expansion may have started 2,000 years ago, but we canceled that
raw_text: Barnes Ice Cap sits on the central plateau of Baffin Island, in the Canadian Arctic. It is the last surviving fragment of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, which at its peak buried most of Canada under two miles of ice and locked away around 80 meters of sea level. That remnant has now yielded direct physical evidence that ice sheets might have reversed their retreat and started to grow again thousands of years ago. In a recent Science study, researchers show that the Laurentide reached its smallest size about 3,600 years ago, then started re-expanding roughly 2,000 years ago, which the team interprets as the opening move of the next glaciation. Apparently, this brand-new ice age was on its way until about 1960, when human-caused climate warming reversed it. Frozen to the bed “Barnes is the last remaining piece of one of the domes of the Laurentide Ice Sheet,” says Nicolás Young, a geologist at Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory and lead author of the study. As that enormous dome thinned through the Holocene, its margin withdrew up onto Baffin Island, and what's left today is the deflated core of something that was once two miles thick. The reason Barnes can testify about its own history, Young explains, comes down to the temperature at its base. Read full article Comments

title: Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads
raw_text: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's a still image, video, audio, or text - that "has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence" to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies , as well as restaurants' ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials.
